Name: compositional_feature_steering
Title: Do Interpretable Features Compose? A Causal Test of Multi-Constraint Steering in Biomolecular Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: If sparse-autoencoder features of protein language models are genuinely disentangled causal handles, then steering along multiple feature directions simultaneously should compose additively—achieving several design constraints at once with minimal interference and preserved validity—whereas raw-activation steering will show destructive interference. We further hypothesize that a feature's interpretability score (concept correlation) does NOT predict its compositional steerability, and we identify what property does.
Related Work: A rapidly growing body of work applies sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to protein language models for single-property steering: InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE (RFdiffusion), MotifAE, ProtoMech (cross-layer transcoders), and antibody/RNA SAEs. Critically, all of these steer toward ONE target property (e.g., a zinc-finger motif, thermostability) and evaluate whether that property appears. The antibody SAE paper (2025) reports the crucial anomaly that high feature-concept correlation does NOT guarantee causal steerability, but does not explain what does or study multi-property control. Our proposal is the first to systematically test COMPOSITIONALITY: whether independently identified feature directions can be combined to satisfy multiple constraints simultaneously, and to establish a predictive theory of which features are compositionally steerable. This distinguishes us from all prior single-target steering work and turns an incidental anomaly into a testable, generalizable principle.
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose protein language model (pLM) activations into human-interpretable features, and recent work shows individual features can steer generation toward single target properties. Real biomolecular design, however, requires satisfying multiple constraints at once (e.g., a specific fold AND high thermostability AND a binding motif). We ask a simple, falsifiable question: do interpretable features COMPOSE? If features are truly disentangled causal handles, steering along several feature directions simultaneously should approximately superpose their individual effects, hitting multiple targets with little interference and preserved sequence validity. We test this on ESM-2 with SAEs trained on its residual stream, defining an Interference Score (degradation of each property when co-steered versus solo) and a Validity Budget (fraction of steering strength before generated sequences become non-viable, measured by pseudo-perplexity, ESMFold pLDDT, and property predictors). Across pairs and triples of properties (secondary-structure content, thermostability proxy, hydrophobicity/GRAVY, catalytic-site motifs), we compare SAE-feature steering, raw-activation steering, and orthogonalized-feature steering. We then test whether a feature's interpretability score predicts its compositional steerability, and propose alternative predictors (activation-space Jacobian alignment, feature monosemanticity under ablation). We expect SAE features to compose more gracefully than raw steering but to exhibit systematic interference clusters, and that steerability is predicted by causal-effect magnitude rather than concept correlation. Results yield a practical recipe for multi-constraint design and a mechanistic account of when interpretable features function as independent design levers.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP (used by every experiment below). Model: frozen ESM-2 650M (33 layers, hidden width 1280) as primary and frozen ESM-2 150M (30 layers, width 640) as a size-robustness check; both are the public facebook/esm masked protein LMs, weights never updated. Interpretability handles: a TopK sparse autoencoder (SAE; k=32 active latents, dictionary 16,384) trained on residual-stream activations at one layer selected by the intrinsic-dimension elbow (expected near the middle block); a Matryoshka SAE is trained as an architecture-robustness variant. SAE training data: 20M residual-stream token-activations sampled from a 500k-sequence subset of UniRef50 (~60M sequences available; 500k chosen to keep one training run under a day on a single A100); Adam, lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, one training pass, 3 SAE seeds. "Steering" = adding alpha times a unit direction (the SAE decoder column, or a baseline direction) to the chosen layer at all positions during masked-infill generation. Property evaluators (all automated, no wet lab): alpha-helix % and beta-sheet % from DSSP run on ESMFold structures; GRAVY hydrophobicity and molecular weight from Biopython; a thermostability proxy from a ridge head fit on the Meltome Atlas (~48k proteins, held-out R^2 reported); two motifs (C2H2 zinc-finger, Ser-His-Asp catalytic triad) via PROSITE regex/HMMER. For each property the single best feature is chosen by concept-correlation on 5k held-out UniRef sequences, giving a bank of ~7 property features. Generation uses 5 sampling seeds; 200 sequences per condition.

Experiment 1 (H1 - additive composition of SAE features): Tests whether co-steering several SAE feature directions at once satisfies several constraints simultaneously with minimal interference and preserved validity. Decisive metric: joint success rate = fraction of generated sequences meeting ALL targeted property thresholds at once. Secondary: per-property Interference Score I = (solo gain - co-steered gain)/solo gain. Convincing result: joint success >= 0.6x the product of the features' solo success rates AND mean I <= 0.2 while the fraction of foldable sequences (ESMFold pLDDT >= 70) falls by < 10 points versus solo steering. Decision band (indeterminate): mean I in [0.2, 0.4] OR joint success in [0.4, 0.6]x the product -> report "partial composition," which neither confirms additive composition nor the destructive alternative, and defer the verdict to the geometric analysis in Experiment 4. Negative result (mean I > 0.4 or joint success < 0.4x product) means SAE features do NOT compose additively, refuting H1. Data/systems: all 21 property PAIRS and 10 TRIPLES from the ~7-feature bank, each co-steered at its solo-calibrated alpha (calibrated by a prior per-feature strength sweep recording property gain vs validity). Robustness: repeat a reduced 3-property protocol on the RiNALMo RNA LM (~650M, frozen) with 2 RNA properties (GC content, a stem-loop motif) to check the compositionality principle transfers across biomolecule type.

Experiment 2 (H2 - raw-activation steering shows destructive interference): Tests the claimed contrast that raw-activation steering interferes where SAE steering does not. Decisive metric: paired difference in mean Interference Score, (raw minus SAE), across the same 21 pairs and 10 triples. Convincing result: raw difference-of-means steering (directions matched to each SAE feature's solo property gain and in norm) shows mean I higher by >= 0.15 with a 95% bootstrap CI excluding 0, and lower joint success. Decision band: difference in [0.0, 0.15] -> the two are indistinguishable on interference; report that SAE features offer no compositional advantage over raw steering (a partial refutation of the framing). Negative result (raw I <= SAE I) refutes H2. Systems compared: (a) additive SAE-feature steering, (b) raw difference-of-means directions, (c) Gram-Schmidt-orthogonalized SAE directions (feeds Experiment 4c).

Experiment 3 (H3 - interpretability score does not predict compositional steerability): Tests whether a feature's concept-correlation predicts how well it composes. Decisive metric: Spearman rho(concept-correlation, compositional steerability), where steerability = 1 - mean I over that feature's pairings. Convincing result for H3 (a null): |rho| <= 0.2 with 95% bootstrap CI contained in [-0.4, 0.4]. Decision band: |rho| in [0.2, 0.4] -> weak, ambiguous predictive value; report as "not clearly predictive." Negative result (rho >= 0.4) means interpretability DOES predict compositional steerability, refuting H3. Data: the ~7-feature bank is small, so we expand it to ~30-40 property-linked features (multiple features per property above a correlation floor) purely to power this regression, reported with n and CIs.

Experiment 4 (H4 - identifying what does predict it, and a geometric fix): Tests the positive companion to H3: that causal-effect magnitude and decoder geometry predict compositional steerability and that pre-orthogonalization repairs interference. (a) Predictor test - decisive metric Spearman rho(causal-effect magnitude, steerability), where causal magnitude = property change per unit alpha at low alpha; convincing if rho >= 0.5 AND exceeds the concept-correlation rho of Experiment 3 by >= 0.2. (b) Interference geometry - decisive metric rho(|decoder-direction cosine|, pairwise Interference Score) across all feature pairs; convincing if rho >= 0.5. (c) Fix - Gram-Schmidt pre-orthogonalize colliding feature pairs and re-run co-steering; convincing if mean I drops by >= 0.15 absolute with joint success rising and validity retained, while we report the interpretability cost (change in the orthogonalized direction's concept-correlation). Decision band: causal rho in [0.3, 0.5], or geometry rho in [0.3, 0.5], or interference reduction in [0.05, 0.15] -> suggestive but not decisive; report the predictor as a candidate needing more features. Negative result (no predictor beats chance and orthogonalization does not reduce interference) means we fail to identify what governs compositional steerability, so the hypothesis's "we identify what property does" clause is unsupported.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Property evaluators (structure/thermostability predictors) are imperfect proxies for wet-lab truth; conclusions are about in-silico controllability, not experimentally validated function. 2) Compositionality may be trivially poor if all chosen features live in a low-dimensional subspace; we mitigate by selecting features spanning diverse concept types and reporting the interference matrix. 3) SAE quality and layer choice could confound results; we control by comparing multiple SAE architectures (TopK, Matryoshka) and model sizes. 4) The predictive-regression analysis could be underpowered if the feature bank is small; we mitigate by including tens of features across properties. 5) Orthogonalization fix may reduce interpretability of steered directions, a tradeoff we will quantify rather than assume away.

Closest prior work is single-target feature steering in protein LMs (InterPLM/ProtSAE/SAE-on-ESM, antibody SAE anomaly). The delta is real and non-trivial: moving from one-property detection/steering to systematic multi-constraint composition and a predictive theory of composition. Name: feature_steering_rare_region_design
Title: Steering Off the Mode: Can Interpretable Features Guide Generative Protein Models Into Rare-but-Valid Design Space?
Short Hypothesis: Interpretable SAE features act as directional handles that let protein language models reach LOW-likelihood-but-still-valid regions of sequence space (rare folds/motifs/property combinations) that likelihood-guided sampling systematically undersamples—and they do so more efficiently and with higher validity than raw activation steering or temperature/top-p sampling. We further hypothesize that a feature's causal steering strength, not its concept-correlation, predicts how far off-mode it can push generation while retaining validity.
Related Work: Existing SAE-and-steering work for protein LMs (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'Steering Protein Language Models'/ASPO 2025; the antibody SAE paper 2025; ProtoMech cross-layer transcoders 2026; Matryoshka SAEs on ESM2-3B 2025) all evaluate whether steering INCREASES a single target property near the model's high-likelihood modes. A recent review (Guiding Generative Models for Protein Design, 2025) explicitly flags that generative models undersample low-probability regions that often encode valuable properties, but proposes no interpretability-based remedy. SAE-Targeted Steering (Chalnev et al. 2024) improves side-effect control in text LMs but does not study distributional escape or rare-region reachability. Our proposal is the first to reframe interpretable-feature steering as a controlled DISTRIBUTION-ESCAPE tool for scientific design: quantifying how far off-mode features can drive valid generation, comparing against non-interpretable exploration baselines, and testing what feature property predicts safe off-mode reach. This turns interpretability from a descriptive add-on into a diversity-and-novelty engine.
Abstract: Generative protein models sample most heavily from the high-likelihood modes of their training distribution, systematically neglecting rare regions of sequence space that may encode novel, valuable designs. Prior interpretability work shows that sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features of protein language models can steer generation toward single target properties, but always tests gains near the model's comfortable modes. We ask a different question: can interpretable features be used as controllable handles to push generation OFF the mode—into low-likelihood but still-valid sequence space—more efficiently and safely than non-interpretable exploration methods? We train SAEs on ESM-2 residual streams and, for each of a bank of property-linked features, sweep steering strength while tracking two quantities jointly: distributional escape (drop in sequence likelihood / distance from natural-sequence manifold) and validity (ESMFold pLDDT, pseudo-perplexity, property-predictor agreement). We define a Reach-Validity Frontier and compare feature steering against raw difference-of-means activation steering, high-temperature/top-p sampling, and random-direction perturbation. We hypothesize that (i) interpretable features achieve a strictly better Reach-Validity frontier than non-directional exploration, (ii) they unlock rare property COMBINATIONS absent from natural training data while remaining foldable, and (iii) a feature's measured causal effect magnitude—not its concept-correlation—predicts how far off-mode it can safely reach. Results would establish interpretable features as an efficient, controllable engine for exploring novel scientific design space, and provide a mechanistic account of which features are trustworthy exploration directions.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models: frozen ESM-2 150M (30 layers, width 640) and ESM-2 650M (33 layers, width 1280), public facebook/esm masked protein LMs, weights frozen. Handles: TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on residual-stream activations at the intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer, plus a Matryoshka SAE for robustness; trained on 20M activation-tokens from a 500k-sequence UniRef50 subset (~60M available; 500k for one-day single-A100 training), Adam lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, 3 SAE seeds. Feature bank: ~30-50 features mapped to measurable properties - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY and molecular weight (Biopython), a thermostability proxy (ridge head on Meltome Atlas ~48k proteins), and 2 motifs (C2H2 zinc-finger, catalytic triad; PROSITE/HMMER). Validity signals: ESMFold pLDDT and pseudo-perplexity thresholds. Generation: 5 seeds, 200 sequences per condition. Off-mode reach for a sequence = its negative log-likelihood under ESM-2 minus the unsteered-baseline mean, combined with embedding kNN distance to its nearest neighbor in a held-out 100k-sequence UniRef sample.

Experiment 1 (H1 - interpretable features dominate the reach-validity frontier): Tests whether SAE-feature steering reaches lower-likelihood but still-valid sequence space than likelihood-based sampling, at higher reach for equal validity than raw-activation steering and than temperature/top-p sampling. Decisive metric: reach-validity frontier area (off-mode reach on one axis, fraction of generations still valid - pLDDT >= 70 and pseudo-perplexity below the natural-set 95th percentile - on the other), per method. Convincing result: SAE-feature frontier area exceeds every baseline by >= 15% relative, paired across features and seeds (95% CI excludes 0), and SAE dominates (higher reach at equal validity) for >= 70% of features. Decision band: relative advantage in [5%, 15%] -> marginal; report SAE as competitive but not clearly dominant. Negative result (< 5% or a baseline on top) refutes H1. Systems: (i) SAE-feature steering, (ii) raw difference-of-means steering, (iii) high-temperature sampling, (iv) top-p sampling, (v) random residual perturbation matched in norm; temperature and top-p are swept over >= 8 settings each to give the strongest fair baseline.

Experiment 2 (H2 - unlocking rare property combinations): Tests whether features generate valid foldable sequences hitting property combinations that are anti-correlated or absent in nature. Decisive metric: valid rare-target success rate = fraction of generations that are valid (pLDDT >= 70), foldable, and simultaneously hit both targeted property bands. Convincing result: SAE steering success >= 2x the best baseline's success AND >= 0.10 in absolute terms (so the win is not 0.01 vs 0.005). Decision band: SAE success between 1.2x and 2x the best baseline -> a real but modest unlock; report as partial support. Negative result (SAE <= 1.2x baseline) refutes H2. Data/targets: 5 target combinations chosen as anti-correlated or unseen in a 100k UniRef sample (e.g., high beta-sheet + high hydrophilicity; two motifs that rarely co-occur), each with 200 generations x 5 seeds; novelty of successes reported as max identity to any natural sequence and embedding distance.

Experiment 3 (H3 - causal steering strength, not concept-correlation, predicts safe off-mode reach): Tests which feature property predicts how far off-mode a feature can push while staying valid. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between a candidate predictor and each feature's frontier area (safe off-mode reach) from Experiment 1. Convincing result: causal-effect magnitude (property change per unit steer near the origin) attains rho >= 0.5 and exceeds concept-correlation's rho by >= 0.2, while concept-correlation's rho lies within [-0.2, 0.2]. Decision band: causal rho in [0.3, 0.5], or its margin over concept-correlation in [0.1, 0.2] -> suggestive only. Negative result (concept-correlation predicts as well as or better than causal magnitude) refutes H3. Predictors also computed: decoder-direction norm/orthogonality to the natural-sequence manifold, and monosemanticity; regression uses the full ~30-50 feature bank with bootstrap CIs. Generalization: a reduced protocol on the p-IgGen antibody LM (~17M) and a GPT-style SMILES molecular LM tests whether frontier dominance transfers across object types.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico validity (ESMFold pLDDT, predictors) is a proxy for wet-lab function; claims are about controllable exploration of model-defined valid space, not experimental viability. 2) 'Off-mode' reach measured by model likelihood may conflate genuinely novel-but-valid sequences with degenerate artifacts; we mitigate via multiple independent validity signals and novelty checks against natural databases. 3) High-temperature baselines may be tuned suboptimally; we sweep them thoroughly to give the strongest fair comparison. 4) The predictor-regression may be underpowered with a modest feature bank; mitigated by using tens of features across property types and multiple seeds. 5) Frontier dominance could be model/SAE-specific; mitigated by testing two model sizes, two SAE architectures, and a cross-domain object type.

The closest prior family is single-target SAE steering for protein LMs (InterPLM/ProtSAE/etc.) plus generic generative exploration baselines (temperature/top-p). The delta is substantive: not just a new property or dataset, but a new objective/phenomenon and evaluation lens. It is still an extension of existing steering rather than a new mechanism, so novelty is strong but not maximal.

Name: steerability_predictor
Title: Decodable but Inert: A Predictive Theory of Which Interpretable Directions Actually Steer Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: Across biomolecular generative models, whether an interpretable/linearly-decodable direction is causally steerable is NOT random noise but is predicted by cheap, intervention-free geometric quantities computed at the intervention site. We hypothesize a specific predictor - the alignment between the direction and the model's local output Jacobian (i.e., how much the downstream computation actually reads that direction) - forecasts steering efficacy far better than concept-correlation or probe accuracy, enabling a pre-flight test that saves expensive generation-based screening.
Related Work: Multiple recent papers independently report the same anomaly: high feature-concept correlation or linear decodability does not guarantee causal steering. The antibody SAE paper (2025) finds TopK SAE features are interpretable but not steerable. The Boltz-1 paper (Jedryszek et al. 2026) finds a beta-strand direction with F1=0.82 that produces zero causal effect. FEGA (Hoang et al. 2026) shows most SAE features lack a stable steering direction and distinguishes value-like vs pointer-like features by their logit-effect geometry. Each treats this as an obstacle or a descriptive taxonomy, and none provides a cheap PREDICTIVE test of steerability nor validates such a predictor as a screening tool across scientific object types. Prior steering work (InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE, ProtoMech, Matryoshka-SAE) demonstrates steering succeeds for SOME directions but selects them by trial-and-error generation. Our proposal turns the shared anomaly into a positive, testable theory: we define candidate intervention-free predictors of steerability, benchmark them against ground-truth steering across models and domains, and demonstrate a Jacobian-alignment 'steerability score' that predicts which directions steer BEFORE any generation. This is a mechanistic advance (why steering fails) and a practical tool (a pre-flight filter), distinct from all prior descriptive or single-direction steering work.
Abstract: A striking anomaly recurs across mechanistic-interpretability studies of scientific generative models: directions that are highly interpretable and linearly decodable frequently produce no causal effect when used to steer generation. Antibody, protein, and structure-prediction studies each independently report this decodable-but-inert phenomenon, yet none explains what distinguishes steerable from inert directions or offers a way to predict steerability before running expensive generation experiments. We propose a predictive theory. Our central hypothesis is that steerability is governed by how strongly the model's downstream computation actually reads a direction at the intervention site, which is captured by the alignment between the direction and the local output Jacobian (the sensitivity of generated properties to activation perturbations). We define a small set of cheap, intervention-free candidate predictors - Jacobian alignment, decoder-direction norm relative to the residual stream, effective read-out via attention/MLP weight projections, and value-like vs pointer-like effect geometry - and benchmark them against ground-truth steering efficacy measured by property change per unit steer. We evaluate across ESM-2 protein LMs, an antibody LM (p-IgGen), and a SMILES molecular LM, using SAE features and difference-of-means directions. We test whether Jacobian alignment predicts steerability with high rank correlation while concept-correlation and probe accuracy do not, and we validate a resulting 'steerability score' as a pre-flight filter that selects effective steering directions without generation, quantifying compute saved. Results would convert a widespread nuisance into an actionable mechanistic principle and a practical screening tool for controllable scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (three families, all frozen): ESM-2 150M and 650M (masked protein LM), p-IgGen antibody LM (~17M), and a GPT-style SMILES molecular LM (~10M, trained on a ~1.9M-molecule ChEMBL subset or a public checkpoint). Directions bank per model: 40-80 strongly decodable directions - TopK SAE features (and Ordered/Matryoshka where available) with high concept-correlation, plus difference-of-means directions for each measurable property. Properties with cheap evaluators: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, motifs (HMMER/regex); antibodies - CDR length, net charge, a developability proxy; molecules - logP, QED, ring count, functional-group presence (RDKit SMARTS). Ground-truth steerability of a direction = slope of target-property change per unit steer at low strength, plus the max reliable property gain before validity collapses (validity: pseudo-perplexity/ESMFold pLDDT for proteins, RDKit-validity for molecules); measured over a strength sweep, 5 generation seeds. For properties with only non-differentiable evaluators (HMMER, folding), a lightweight differentiable surrogate predictor supplies the Jacobian; surrogate held-out fidelity (R^2/AUROC) is reported.

Experiment 1 (H1+H2 - a cheap geometric quantity predicts steerability better than concept-correlation): Tests that causal steerability is non-randomly predicted by intervention-free geometry, and specifically that Jacobian alignment beats concept-correlation/probe accuracy. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between each candidate predictor and ground-truth steerability, with bootstrap CIs, per model and pooled. Negative result (concept-correlation predicts as well as Jacobian alignment) refutes H2; if NO predictor beats rho 0.3, steerability is closer to noise, refuting H1. Experiment 2 (H2 - causal test via synthetic directions): Tests whether Jacobian alignment causes steerability rather than merely correlating. Convincing result: precision@10 >= 0.8, at least 2x the concept-correlation ranking and above random, with compute saved (generation runs avoided to find 10 good directions) >= 50%. Decision band: precision@10 in [0.5, 0.8] -> a useful but imperfect screen. Negative result (precision@10 <= random) refutes H3. Reported per model.

Decisive metric: the Experiment-1 Spearman rho within each family. Convincing result: rho >= 0.4 in all three families. Negative result (holds in only one family) means the principle is family-specific, a scientifically informative limit rather than a universal law.

Name: intervention_leak_scientific_design
Title: Does Clamping Fix It? Auditing Whether Interpretable-Feature Interventions Truly Eliminate Undesired Properties in Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: When we clamp/ablate an interpretable feature to REMOVE an undesired property (a toxic substructure, an instability motif, a disallowed fold) from a scientific generative model, the model often reconstitutes that property through alternative internal routes during iterative/autoregressive decoding. We hypothesize that feature-level suppression frequently 'leaks': the property re-emerges in the final object at rates that concept-correlation and single-forward-pass evidence would deem impossible, and this leakage is predictable from the redundancy (number of alternative encoding features) of the target concept.
Related Work: Almost all interpretability-for-design work (InterPLM, ProtSAE, FoldSAE, molecular-transformer SAE circuits, GFlowNet interpretation, chemical-LM steering vector fields, molecular task arithmetic) demonstrates that clamping/steering a feature CHANGES a target property, and reports success at the level of a forward pass or a single generation. A concurrent text-LLM paper (Cui et al. 2026, 'SAE Interventions are Unreliable: Post-Intervention Recovery') shows clamping an 'unsafe' feature in language models can be optimized around, revealing that suppression blocks one visible route but not the behavior. No prior work asks whether feature interventions ROBUSTLY eliminate undesired properties in SCIENTIFIC generative models, where 'recovery' is an objectively measurable structural fact (a toxic SMILES substructure appears; a destabilizing motif is present; a forbidden secondary structure forms) rather than fuzzy text behavior, and where the multi-step, structured decoding process (autoregressive SMILES, iterative diffusion denoising) provides many natural re-routing opportunities. We are the first to (i) define and measure intervention leakage for scientific object design, (ii) test whether it arises spontaneously during ordinary generation (not just adversarial optimization), and (iii) tie leakage to concept redundancy, yielding a practical audit + a redundancy-aware multi-feature clamping fix.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design increasingly relies on a hopeful assumption: that clamping or ablating an interpretable feature reliably removes the property it encodes. We stress-test this assumption for scientific generative models, where 'the property' is an objectively verifiable structural fact—a toxic substructure in a molecule, a destabilizing motif in a protein, or a disallowed fold. We define intervention leakage as the rate at which a suppressed, undesirable property reappears in the final generated object despite an active feature-level intervention. Using autoregressive SMILES chemical language models and ESM-2 protein language models with sparse autoencoders, we clamp features that a forward-pass analysis identifies as encoding a target undesired property, then run ordinary iterative generation and check the finished object with hard structural evaluators (RDKit substructure matching, HMMER/regex motifs, DSSP/ESMFold). We hypothesize that leakage is substantial and, crucially, arises during normal decoding rather than only under adversarial optimization, because the model can re-encode the concept through alternative features at later positions/denoising steps. We further hypothesize that leakage is predicted by concept redundancy—the number of SAE features (or the effective rank of the concept subspace) that encode the target property—and we validate a redundancy-aware fix that clamps the full concept subspace rather than a single feature. We report leakage rates, a redundancy-based predictor of intervention reliability, and the validity cost of subspace clamping. Results turn feature interventions from an assumed-safe knob into an auditable, quantifiable one, with direct implications for safe and reliable scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (both frozen): (a) a GPT-style autoregressive SMILES chemical LM (~10M, trained on a ChEMBL/ZINC subset, or a public checkpoint) with a TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream at a mid layer; (b) ESM-2 150M/650M (masked protein LM) with a residual-stream TopK SAE. SAEs trained on 20M activation-tokens (500k-sequence/molecule subset), Adam lr 1e-3, batch 4,096, 3 SAE seeds. Undesired properties chosen to have HARD, model-independent evaluators: for molecules, presence of specific PAINS/toxicophore substructures, a reactive group, or exceeding a ring/heteroatom bound (RDKit SMARTS); for proteins, a specific catalytic/binding motif (HMMER/regex) and a secondary-structure target (DSSP on ESMFold). For each property, the single best encoding feature and the ranked set of features above a concept-correlation floor (the candidate concept subspace) are recorded via concept-correlation and probe AUROC on held-out objects. "Clamp" = fixing the feature to a strong suppressive value at every decoding step. Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - feature suppression leaks in the finished object): Tests whether clamping the best feature to remove a property still lets the property appear in finished objects at rates that single-forward-pass evidence would deem impossible. Decisive metric: the forward-pass-vs-end-object gap = (Leakage Rate) minus (the residual property rate implied by the clamp's single-step logit/probe suppression), where Leakage Rate = fraction of FINISHED objects that still contain the property under the hard evaluator despite the active clamp. Convincing result: this gap >= 20 percentage points for at least half of the target properties. Decision band: gap in [10, 20] points -> leakage present but modest; report as partial support. Negative result (gap < 10 points, i.e. leakage close to what forward-pass suppression predicts) means interventions are reliable - a valuable positive result about intervention fidelity, refuting the leak hypothesis. Data/systems: N = 2,000 objects per property, generated under conditions that naturally exhibit the property (property-biased sampling/seed contexts); compared against (i) no intervention (baseline occurrence) and (ii) the single-forward-pass "success" estimate. A re-routing trace on leaked objects (when the property re-emerges, and which alternative features carry high concept-probe activation there) plus one-by-one ablation of those features confirming leakage drops identifies the leak paths.

Experiment 2 (H2 - redundancy predicts leakage): Tests that leakage is predictable from how redundantly the concept is encoded. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between per-property Leakage Rate and a redundancy score (number of features above the correlation floor; effective rank of the concept subspace via SVD of correlated-feature activation vectors; probe accuracy retained after removing the top feature). Convincing result: redundancy rho >= 0.5 (CI excludes 0) while single-feature concept-correlation shows rho within [-0.2, 0.2]. Decision band: redundancy rho in [0.3, 0.5] -> suggestive. Negative result (redundancy no more predictive than concept-correlation) refutes H2. Data: tens of target properties per domain (many toxicophores/motifs) to power the regression, bootstrap CIs.

Experiment 3 (H3 - redundancy-aware suppression closes the leak): Tests that clamping the full concept subspace, not one feature, removes the leak - the causal confirmation of the redundancy mechanism. Decisive metric: Leakage Rate as a function of subspace dimension k (projecting out the top-k correlated directions). Convincing result: Leakage Rate falls monotonically with k and drops below 5% at a modest k (say k <= 8) while the validity cost stays acceptable (RDKit-validity / pseudo-perplexity / ESMFold pLDDT within 10% of baseline and bounded off-target property drift). Decision band: leakage reaches [5%, 15%] only at large k, or the k needed incurs a validity cost beyond 10% -> the fix works but at a real price; report the leakage-validity frontier. Negative result (subspace clamping does not reduce leakage below single-feature clamping) undercuts the redundancy account. Generalization: repeat a reduced protocol on a masked/diffusion generation setting to test whether iterative denoising leaks differently than autoregressive decoding.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Hard evaluators define the property crisply, but choosing properties with unambiguous structural evaluators limits generality to such properties; fuzzy properties (e.g., 'developability') are out of scope. 2) Leakage could be an artifact of weak clamping strength; we mitigate by sweeping clamp magnitude up to the point of validity collapse and reporting leakage across the whole range. 3) SAE quality and layer choice may confound which features 'encode' the property; we control with multiple SAE architectures/layers and probe-based verification. 4) In-silico validity and property calls (ESMFold, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab truth; claims concern model-internal controllability and structural facts, not experimental function. 5) The redundancy predictor could be underpowered with few target properties; we mitigate by including many properties per domain (tens of toxicophores/motifs). 6) If leakage turns out to be negligible, that is still a scientifically valuable positive result establishing intervention reliability, and the redundancy analysis explains why.

Name: interpretable_feature_bayesopt
Title: Optimizing in Concept Space: Do Interpretable SAE Features Make Scientific Design Optimization More Sample-Efficient and Auditable?
Short Hypothesis: Running Bayesian optimization directly over the sparse, monosemantic feature space of a sparse autoencoder trained on a frozen scientific foundation model yields more sample-efficient design than BO over the model's raw embeddings or a VAE latent space, AND provides human-readable design rationales. We further hypothesize that the per-dimension monosemanticity of the search space (not merely its dimensionality) is what predicts optimization efficiency, and that interpretability enables concept-prior warm-starting that further cuts oracle calls.
Related Work: Latent-space Bayesian optimization (LSBO) is a mature line: Automatic Chemical Design (Gomez-Bombarelli 2018), Constrained BO in VAE latent space (Griffiths & Hernandez-Lobato 2019), LaMBO (Stanton 2022), CLaSMO (2024), and low-dimensional semi-supervised latent BO for antimicrobial peptides (2025). Separately, SAE-steering work (InterPLM 2024, ProtSAE 2025, 'SAEs for Low-N Protein Function Prediction and Design' 2025, Steering Protein LMs/ASPO 2025) shows SAE latents can steer generation and even design high-fitness variants via manual latent steering. The crucial gap: (i) no prior work uses the INTERPRETABLE SAE feature space of a FROZEN foundation model as the actual optimization search space for closed-loop, oracle-guided Bayesian optimization; existing LSBO uses black-box VAE/embedding spaces, and the low-N SAE paper uses manual/greedy steering, not query-efficient BO with uncertainty. (ii) No one has tested whether the MONOSEMANTICITY of the search space is causally responsible for optimization efficiency, versus mere dimensionality reduction. (iii) No one exploits interpretability to warm-start BO with concept-property priors or to emit human-readable design trajectories. Our proposal isolates the value of interpretability as a search-space property, distinguishing it from generic dimensionality reduction, and from all prior LSBO and SAE-steering work.
Abstract: Scientific design—of proteins, molecules, and sequences—is a query-efficiency problem: each oracle evaluation is expensive, so the geometry of the search space matters. Latent-space Bayesian optimization (LSBO) searches the black-box latent of a task-specific VAE, while recent interpretability work shows sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose frozen foundation-model activations into monosemantic, concept-aligned features. We unify these threads and ask: does optimizing directly in an interpretable SAE feature space improve sample efficiency and auditability compared to optimizing in raw embeddings or a VAE latent? We build a closed-loop pipeline where a Gaussian-process surrogate proposes points in the SAE feature space of a frozen ESM-2 (proteins) or a SMILES chemical language model, decodes them back to residual-stream activations, and generates candidate objects scored by cheap in-silico oracles. We compare against embedding-space BO, VAE-latent LSBO (LaMBO-style), and genetic-algorithm baselines under matched oracle budgets. Our central scientific test is whether per-dimension monosemanticity, not just dimensionality, drives efficiency: we construct search spaces with matched dimension but varied monosemanticity (SAE features vs. random rotations vs. PCA) and correlate monosemanticity with optimization regret. We further exploit interpretability two ways: concept-prior warm-starting (initializing the GP mean from known feature-property associations) and human-readable design trajectories (reporting which named concepts each optimization step turned up or down). We expect interpretable-feature BO to match or beat baselines in regret-at-budget while additionally yielding auditable, controllable design paths—turning interpretability from a descriptive luxury into a concrete optimization asset.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Encoders (frozen): for proteins, ESM-2 150M/650M with a TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream at the intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer; for molecules, a GPT-style SMILES chemical LM (~10M) with a residual-stream SAE. Encoding: object -> foundation-model activations -> SAE feature vector (mean-pooled). Decoding: SAE feature vector -> reconstructed activations -> object (masked infilling / activation-conditioned decoding for proteins; activation steering during autoregressive decoding for SMILES). Encode-decode round-trip fidelity (property-preservation rate on a held-out set) is verified and reported before optimization. Oracles (cheap): proteins - ESMFold pLDDT (validity), DSSP secondary-structure targets, GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability/fitness head, and FLIP/ProteinGym fitness tasks where available; molecules - RDKit logP, QED, penalized-logP, docking against one fixed target, synthetic accessibility. Every reported optimization run uses >= 20 random seeds.

Experiment 1 (H1 - SAE-space BO is more sample-efficient): Tests whether Bayesian optimization over the SAE feature space finds better designs per oracle call than BO over raw embeddings or a VAE latent. Decisive metric: oracle-calls-to-threshold (calls to first reach a fixed target property value), median over >= 20 seeds and multiple target properties; secondary regret-at-budget. Convincing result: SAE-space BO needs >= 30% fewer oracle calls than the best competing space, with the paired 95% CI excluding a tie. Decision band: reduction in [10%, 30%] -> a real but modest efficiency gain. Negative result (< 10% or slower) refutes H1. Systems, identical GP+Expected-Improvement (qEI for batches) and identical oracle budget: (a) SAE feature space, (b) raw foundation-model embeddings PCA-reduced to the SAE's active dimension (isolating space identity from dimension), (c) a task-trained VAE latent (LaMBO-style), (d) a discrete genetic algorithm on the object. Validity retention along the trajectory and novelty/diversity of optima also reported.

Experiment 2 (H3 - monosemanticity, not dimensionality, drives efficiency): Tests the central claim by holding dimensionality fixed and varying only per-axis meaning. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between a per-space monosemanticity score (mean per-feature concept-correlation / activation sparsity) and optimization efficiency (area over the regret curve), across matched-dimension spaces and target properties. Convincing result: rho >= 0.5 at fixed dimension. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.5] -> suggestive. Negative result (rho within [-0.2, 0.2]) means dimensionality, not monosemanticity, was doing the work, refuting H3. Matched-dimension spaces: (i) SAE features (high monosemanticity), (ii) a random rotation of the SAE basis (same geometry/dimension, meaning destroyed), (iii) PCA components (dense, mixed), (iv) a partially trained/entangled SAE.

Experiment 3 (H4 - concept-prior warm-starting cuts oracle calls, only in the interpretable space): Tests whether known feature-property associations can warm-start the search. Decisive metric: oracle-calls-to-threshold, warm-start vs cold-start, in the SAE space. Convincing result: >= 25% fewer calls warm vs cold, and the baseline spaces (which lack named axes) cannot be warm-started the same way. Decision band: reduction in [10%, 25%] -> modest speedup. Negative result (no warm-start benefit) refutes H4. Warm-start initializes the GP prior mean / restricts the initial design region using concept-correlation associations; reported with and without label filtering to expose sensitivity to noisy labels.

Experiment 4 (H2 - auditable, faithful design rationales): Tests whether the interpretable space yields human-readable rationales that are actually faithful. Decisive metric: trajectory-faithfulness score = fraction of reported concept-changes whose ablation reproduces the predicted property-change direction. Convincing result: faithfulness >= 0.7, a deliverable the raw-embedding/VAE/GA baselines cannot produce at all. Decision band: faithfulness in [0.5, 0.7] -> partially trustworthy rationales. Negative result (< 0.5) means the rationales are post-hoc and unreliable, refuting the auditability claim. Each accepted BO step emits the top named concepts increased/decreased (annotation- or LLM-labeled) and the resulting property change. The full protocol is repeated across both domains and two model sizes for robustness.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico oracles are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern sample-efficiency and auditability of optimization, not experimental validation. 2) SAE encode/decode round-trip fidelity may be lossy, capping achievable optima; we quantify reconstruction quality and report its correlation with performance, and use the best available SAE architecture. 3) The interpretable space could win merely by favorable dimensionality; the matched-dimension monosemanticity experiment (step 4) is specifically designed to rule this out. 4) GP surrogates scale poorly to very high feature dimensions; we mitigate with sparsity-aware feature selection (optimize only over active/relevant features) and additive/trust-region GPs, reporting sensitivity to this choice. 5) Concept-prior warm-starting depends on the quality of feature-property labels, which may be noisy; we report warm-start gains with and without label filtering. 6) If interpretable-feature BO merely ties baselines on regret, the auditability and warm-start results still constitute a meaningful, publishable contribution establishing interpretability as a 'free' optimization asset.

Name: cross_model_steering_transfer
Title: Steer Small, Design Big: Transferring Validated Interpretable Steering Directions Across Scientific Generative Models
Short Hypothesis: Because SAE feature spaces are approximately universal across models (similar under rotation-invariant alignment), a steering direction that is discovered and causally VALIDATED on a small, cheap generative model can be aligned and transferred to steer a larger or different-architecture model to produce objects with the same target property—without re-running expensive steerability screening on the big model. We further hypothesize that transferred directions inherit not just the target effect but also the small model's causal steerability, so cheap models can serve as steerability-screening proxies for expensive ones.
Related Work: Two lines converge here. (1) SAE steering of scientific generative models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; Steering PLMs/ASPO 2025; ProtoMech cross-layer transcoders 2026; SAEs for low-N design 2025) all discover and validate steering directions SEPARATELY per model, requiring costly per-model SAE training and generation-based screening. (2) Feature-space universality work (Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across LLMs via SAEs, 2024) shows SAE feature subspaces are similar across text LLMs under rotation-invariant transforms and conjectures—but never demonstrates for generation—that steering vectors might transfer. No prior work (a) tests whether interpretable steering directions transfer BETWEEN scientific generative models to control the properties of GENERATED objects, (b) exploits a cheap model as a steerability-screening proxy for an expensive one, or (c) quantifies the design-efficiency savings of not re-discovering steerable features per model. The concurrent DiMaS (2026) finding that features are 'linearly decodable but not linearly steerable' makes the transfer-of-steerability question especially non-trivial and worth testing. Our proposal turns universality from a descriptive observation into a practical cross-model design tool.
Abstract: Steering interpretable features to control generated proteins, molecules, and other scientific objects currently requires expensive, model-specific pipelines: train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), screen thousands of features for which ones actually steer, and validate on the target model. As foundation models grow, this per-model cost dominates. We ask whether this cost can be paid once on a small model and amortized: given evidence that SAE feature spaces are approximately universal across models, can a steering direction discovered and causally validated on a small, cheap generative model be aligned and transferred to steer a larger or different-architecture model? We build a cross-model transfer pipeline: (1) discover and causally validate steering directions on a small model (e.g., ESM-2 35M) using cheap in-silico property oracles; (2) learn a rotation/linear alignment between the small and large models' representation spaces from paired activations on a shared held-out corpus; (3) map the validated direction into the large model and steer generation. We evaluate on protein LMs across sizes (ESM-2 35M→150M→650M) and across architectures (masked ESM-2 ↔ autoregressive protein LM), plus a molecular SMILES LM pair. Metrics: property-gain transfer efficiency (fraction of native steering effect recovered), validity retention (ESMFold pLDDT, RDKit validity, pseudo-perplexity), and—crucially—whether a direction's steerability on the small model predicts its steerability on the large one, enabling cheap steerability screening. Success would let practitioners screen and validate design controls on inexpensive models and deploy them on state-of-the-art ones, cutting the compute cost of controllable scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Protein models (frozen): ESM-2 at 35M, 150M, 650M (same family, three sizes) and an autoregressive protein LM (ProtGPT2 or p-IgGen) for cross-architecture transfer. Molecule models: two GPT-style SMILES LMs of different sizes/tokenizers. Oracles: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability proxy (light fine-tuned head), motifs (HMMER/regex, e.g. zinc-finger); molecules - RDKit logP, QED, ring count, functional-group presence. Validity: ESMFold pLDDT and pseudo-perplexity (proteins), RDKit-validity (molecules). Source-model discovery: TopK SAEs (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the small model's residual stream (intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer); per property, candidate directions (SAE features + difference-of-means) are causally validated by a strength sweep measuring property gain vs validity, recording each direction's native steerability. Alignment map T between source and target residual spaces is learned from paired per-position activations on a shared held-out corpus (Procrustes/ridge, plus a rotation-invariant variant), with alignment quality reported as SVCCA and held-out reconstruction R^2; sensitivity to paired-corpus size is swept. Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - a validated direction transfers to steer the larger/other model): Tests whether a direction discovered and causally validated on the cheap model, mapped through T, steers the target model to the same property without re-screening on the target. Decisive metric: Transfer Efficiency TE = (target property gain from the transferred direction) / (target property gain from a direction natively discovered and validated on the target). Convincing result: TE >= 0.7 for same-family size pairs and >= 0.5 for cross-architecture pairs, each exceeding all controls. Decision band: TE in [0.4, 0.7] (same-family) or [0.3, 0.5] (cross-architecture) -> partial transfer; report as usable-with-loss. Negative result (TE < 0.4 same-family, or < 0.3 cross-architecture, or not above controls) refutes H1 for that regime. Systems/controls: (a) random-direction transfer through T, (b) naive same-index feature transfer without alignment, (c) no steering; tested across all size pairs, cross-architecture pairs, and the molecular pair. Absolute property gain, validity retention, and novelty/diversity also reported.

Experiment 2 (H2 - cheap models as steerability-screening proxies): Tests whether source-model steerability predicts target-model steerability, so the small model can pre-select which directions will steer the big one. Decisive metric: Spearman rho between source-model native steerability and target-model steerability of the transferred direction (and of the natively rediscovered counterpart). Convincing result: rho >= 0.5, with precision@10 >= 0.7 for using the small model to pick the target's steerable directions, and compute saved (big-model generation runs avoided to find 10 good directions) >= 50%. Decision band: rho in [0.3, 0.5] or precision@10 in [0.5, 0.7] -> a useful but noisy proxy. Negative result (rho <= 0.3 or precision@10 near random) refutes H2. Decisive metric: joint constraint-satisfaction rate on the target under transferred directions, versus the same on natively validated directions. Convincing result: transferred joint satisfaction >= 0.7x the native joint satisfaction with comparable interference. Decision band: [0.4, 0.7]x -> partial preservation. Negative result (< 0.4x) means transfer does not carry compositional control. Name: causal_timing_window_design
Title: The Right Feature at the Right Time: Causal Intervention Windows for Interpretable Control of Biomolecular Diffusion Models
Short Hypothesis: During iterative diffusion generation of proteins and molecules, each interpretable feature has a distinct CAUSAL WINDOW—a range of denoising timesteps where clamping it actually decides the corresponding property, outside of which the same intervention is inert or destroys validity. We hypothesize (i) property classes stratify by window (coarse/topological properties are decided early, fine/local properties late), and (ii) intervening only inside a feature's causal window achieves the target property with far higher validity and far fewer wasted intervention steps than the standard practice of applying steering uniformly across all timesteps or at a single pass.
Related Work: Image-diffusion interpretability shows temporally-structured concept emergence: 'Emergence and Evolution of Interpretable Concepts in Diffusion Models' (2025) finds composition locks in early and style mid-process; TIDE (2025) builds temporal-aware SAEs; 'Unraveling the Temporal Dynamics of the Unet' (2023) finds composition/denoising phases. DLM-Scope (2026) does diffusion-time SAE steering for text but does not characterize property-specific causal windows. In the scientific-object space, all steering work (InterPLM 2024, ProtSAE 2025, ProtoMech 2026, antibody-SAE 2025, automated-neuron-labelling 2025) either uses masked/autoregressive models with single-pass interventions or applies steering uniformly, and none studies WHEN during a diffusion denoising trajectory an interpretable feature is causally decisive for a hard, verifiable property. The protein-DPO paper (2026) reports a training-time temporal decoupling of structure vs property, but concerns fine-tuning dynamics, not inference-time feature interventions. We are the first to (a) map property-class-specific causal intervention windows for interpretable features in biomolecular diffusion generation, (b) show that window-targeted intervention beats uniform/single-pass steering on the validity–control frontier, and (c) turn timing into an efficiency lever (fewer intervention steps, cheaper compute) for scientific design.
Abstract: Interpretability-guided design of proteins and molecules increasingly relies on clamping interpretable features to control target properties, but nearly all methods apply the intervention with the same strength at every step of the generative process. Work on image diffusion has shown that interpretable concepts emerge and lock in at different stages—composition early, style later—implying that WHEN you intervene matters as much as WHAT you intervene on. We ask whether biomolecular diffusion models exhibit analogous property-specific causal windows and whether exploiting them makes controllable scientific design more valid and efficient. Using discrete/continuous protein diffusion models and a SMILES/graph molecular diffusion model, we train sparse autoencoders on their per-timestep denoiser activations, identify features linked to hard, verifiable properties (secondary-structure content, fold topology, motifs for proteins; ring systems, functional groups, logP-band for molecules), and measure each feature's causal effect on the finished object when clamped only within a sliding timestep window. This yields a Causal Timing Map. We test two hypotheses: (1) property classes stratify by window—coarse/topological properties are decided early, fine/local properties late; (2) window-targeted intervention Pareto-dominates uniform and single-pass steering on a control–validity frontier while using far fewer intervention steps. We report timing maps, frontier comparisons, an efficiency accounting of intervention steps saved, and a simple scheduling recipe that assigns each desired property to its causal window. Results would establish timing as a first-class, efficiency-boosting control axis for interpretable scientific design.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Generators (both instrumentable for per-step denoiser activations, frozen): (a) a discrete/masked protein diffusion or order-agnostic protein LM (a masked-diffusion ESM-style model or a DPLM-type model) and (b) a molecular diffusion model over SMILES/graphs. Hard automated evaluators so "the property in the finished object" is unambiguous: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), a fold-topology/contact-order proxy, GRAVY, molecular weight, motifs (HMMER/regex, e.g. zinc-finger); molecules - ring count / aromatic-ring presence, specific functional groups (RDKit SMARTS), a logP band, QED. Validity gates: ESMFold pLDDT and pseudo-perplexity (proteins); RDKit-validity and synthetic accessibility (molecules). Temporal SAEs: TopK SAEs (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the denoiser residual stream, both a timestep-shared variant and a temporally-conditioned (TIDE-style) variant, at the intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer; reconstruction fidelity and per-timestep concept-correlation with each hard property reported on held-out generations. "Clamp within a window" = fixing a feature to a strong value only for timesteps inside a specified window. Generation seeds: 5; 200 objects per condition.

Experiment 1 (H1 - each feature has a distinct causal window): Tests whether clamping a property-linked feature decides the finished-object property only inside a specific timestep window and is inert or destructive outside it. Decisive metric: window-localized causal effect = property change in the finished object per intervened step, as a function of window position/width (the Causal Timing Map). Convincing result: for >= 70% of property features there exists a window whose per-step effect is >= 2x the effect of clamping uniformly across the whole trajectory, AND clamping only outside that window changes the property by < 25% of the in-window effect. Decision band: an above-baseline window exists but its per-step effect is only 1.3-2x uniform -> weak localization; report as partial support. Negative result (no window beats uniform clamping) refutes H1. Data: non-overlapping timestep bins covering the trajectory plus growing/shrinking windows, per feature, with strength swept inside each window so timing effects are reported controlling for steering strength.

Experiment 2 (H2a - properties stratify by window: coarse early, fine late): Tests whether coarse/topological properties are decided earlier than fine/local ones. Decisive metric: difference in mean causal-window center (as a fraction of the trajectory) between coarse properties (fold class, overall structure content, scaffold ring system) and fine ones (a single motif, one functional group), from a mixed-effects regression of window-center on property class. Convincing result: coarse centers earlier by >= 15% of the trajectory with the 95% CI excluding 0, in both domains. Decision band: difference in [5%, 15%] of the trajectory -> a trend, not decisive. Negative or reversed result (fine decided as early or earlier) refutes H2a but is still an informative characterization. We also test whether window center aligns with when the feature's concept-correlation first becomes predictive of the final object during unsteered generation.

Experiment 3 (H2b - window-targeted intervention dominates uniform/single-pass and saves steps): Tests whether intervening only inside each feature's mapped window beats standard uniform or single-pass steering. Decisive metric: control-validity frontier area (property success rate vs validity retention). Convincing result: window-targeted steering dominates the frontier AND uses >= 40% fewer intervention steps than uniform steering at matched property success. Decision band: frontier parity but >= 40% fewer steps, OR frontier dominance with < 40% step savings -> a partial win on one axis; report both. Negative result (no frontier or efficiency advantage) refutes H2b. Systems: (a) uniform steering across all timesteps, (b) single-pass/late-only steering, (c) window-targeted steering. Multi-property scheduling: for 2-3 properties with different windows, assign each to its own window and test whether temporal separation lowers interference versus co-applying all interventions at every step. Robustness across both domains, two checkpoints/sizes, and shared vs temporally-conditioned SAEs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Requires generators with accessible per-step activations; if a target model's diffusion process is not easily instrumented we substitute alternatives, limiting generality to instrumentable models. 2) In-silico evaluators (ESMFold, DSSP, RDKit) are proxies for wet-lab function; claims concern model-internal causal timing and controllability, not experimental viability. 3) Causal windows may be entangled with steering strength; we sweep strength within each window and report timing effects controlling for strength. 4) Temporally-shared SAEs may blur timestep-specific features; we mitigate with temporally-conditioned SAEs and report differences. 5) The stratification hypothesis could fail (some fine properties decided early); a null or reversed result is still an informative, publishable characterization. 6) Feature-property linkage relies on concept-correlation, which can be non-causal; the sliding-window clamp is itself the causal test, so we treat correlation only as a candidate-selection step. 7) Efficiency gains depend on how much of the trajectory the causal window occupies; if windows are broad, savings shrink—this is directly quantified rather than assumed.

Name: internal_validity_foresight
Title: Failure Foresight: Do Interpretable Features Predict Invalid Scientific Generations Early Enough to Abort and Save Compute?
Short Hypothesis: During iterative/autoregressive generation of proteins and molecules, a small set of interpretable sparse-autoencoder features acts as an early internal 'validity alarm' that predicts, well before generation completes, whether the finished object will be invalid (unfoldable, chemically invalid, degenerate). Related Work: A large body of interpretability work uses SAE features to detect and mitigate hallucinations in text and vision-language models (RAGLens 2025; SSL/SAVE/SAFE 2025; 'Do I Know This Entity?' 2024; H-Neurons 2025) and to detect hallucinations early from internal states in factual QA (Varshney et al. 2024; MHAD 2024; HaMI 2025; HD-NDEs 2025). Separately, interpretability-for-design work on proteins/molecules (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; ProtoMech 2026; molecular-LM SAEs) focuses on STEERING features to add properties, and evaluates validity only as a side constraint. No prior work (a) treats interpretable features as a predictive EARLY-WARNING signal for the objective, structurally-verifiable INVALIDITY of a to-be-generated scientific object, (b) uses that signal to drive an early-abort-and-restart policy that improves valid-yield-per-compute, or (c) compares such interpretable monitoring against output-probability/perplexity early-stopping baselines on a compute-efficiency frontier. We convert the 'model self-knowledge' insight from the text-hallucination literature into a concrete, compute-saving reliability tool for scientific design, where validity is an unambiguous physical/chemical fact rather than fuzzy factuality.
Abstract: Generative models for scientific design frequently emit invalid objects—proteins that do not fold, molecules that violate chemistry, degenerate sequences—and practitioners discover this only after paying the full cost of generation and validation. We ask whether a model's own interpretable internal features reveal, early in generation, that it is heading toward an invalid object, and whether acting on that signal can save substantial compute. Building on evidence from language models that sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features encode a form of self-knowledge, we train SAEs on the intermediate activations of protein and molecular generative models and search for a compact set of features whose early activations predict the eventual validity of the finished object, verified by hard structural evaluators (ESMFold pLDDT and pseudo-perplexity for proteins; RDKit validity and synthetic-accessibility for molecules). We characterize how early and how accurately these 'validity-alarm' features forecast failure, and whether they are interpretable (e.g., firing on frustrated partial structures or chemically inconsistent fragments). We then deploy them in an early-abort-and-restart controller that terminates doomed generations and reallocates the saved budget, measuring valid objects produced per unit compute against three baselines: run-to-completion, output-probability/perplexity early stopping, and a black-box probe on raw activations. Our central claims are that (i) interpretable features predict eventual invalidity earlier and more accurately than output-side signals, and (ii) an interpretability-driven abort policy Pareto-dominates baselines on the valid-yield-versus-compute frontier while yielding human-readable failure diagnoses. Results would establish interpretable features as a practical reliability-and-efficiency layer for scientific generation.

SHARED SETUP. Generators (instrumentable for per-step activations, frozen): (a) a protein generator - an autoregressive protein LM (ProtGPT2/p-IgGen) and/or a masked-diffusion protein LM; (b) a molecular generator - a GPT-style SMILES LM and/or a SMILES/graph diffusion model. Hard automatic VALIDITY labels for finished objects: proteins - ESMFold pLDDT above threshold AND pseudo-perplexity below threshold AND non-degenerate (low repeat/entropy); molecules - RDKit parseable/valence-valid AND passing basic sanity (SA score, ring/atom-count bounds). Corpus: 20k generations per model under normal sampling, saving full per-step activation trajectories, giving a balanced valid/invalid set. TopK SAEs (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream at a mid layer (intrinsic-dimension-elbow). At each progress fraction (10/25/50/75%) each SAE feature's mutual information / AUROC about eventual validity is measured on a training split, and a compact "validity-alarm" feature set is selected by information; all thresholds are fixed on a held-out split. Generation seeds: 5.

Name: causal_correlational_discrepancy
Title: When the Model Disagrees with the Textbook: Using Interpretable-Feature Interventions to Discover Causal Structure-Property Rules That Contradict Correlational Biophysics
Short Hypothesis: Sparse-autoencoder features of scientific foundation models encode two kinds of structure-property associations: those that merely reflect correlations in training data, and those the model uses causally during generation. By comparing a feature's CORRELATIONAL association with a property (how often it co-occurs) against its CAUSAL effect (what happens to the generated object's property when it is clamped), we can systematically surface DISCREPANT features - cases where a well-established correlational structure-property rule is not causally exploited by the model, or where the model imposes a causal rule with no known correlational basis. We hypothesize such discrepancies are numerous, are enriched for genuine confounded/non-causal rules (validated against physics-based counterfactuals), and constitute a hypothesis-generation engine for design rules.
Related Work: Two lines are relevant. (1) SAE feature discovery in scientific models (InterPLM 2024; ProtSAE 2025; 'From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology' 2025; the chemistry-LM SAE 2025; motif-gated domain-recognition causal patching 2025) shows features correlate with biological/chemical concepts and that some are causally necessary for a PREDICTION task. (2) Latent causal discovery (PerturbLearn attribute graphs 2022; active causal ML for molecules 2024) extracts causal graphs among attributes. Crucially, all discovery work either (a) reports concept-CORRELATION of features, or (b) verifies causal effect for a single prediction task, but NO work systematically contrasts a feature's correlational property-association with its causal generative effect to identify DISCREPANCIES, nor uses those discrepancies as a filter for finding structure-property rules that are correlational-but-not-causal (spurious) versus causal-but-uncatalogued (novel). Prior steering work treats agreement between correlation and causation as assumed; we treat their DISAGREEMENT as the scientific signal. This reframes interpretability from cataloguing what the model represents to auditing which structure-property rules are actually causal, and validates the model's verdicts against independent physics-based counterfactuals - a genuinely new use of feature interventions.
Abstract: Structure-property rules are the backbone of protein and molecular design, yet many textbook rules are correlational and may not reflect causal mechanism. Scientific foundation models have absorbed enormous data and, through sparse autoencoders (SAEs), expose interpretable features linked to structural and property concepts. We propose to use these features to audit structure-property rules by contrasting two quantities per feature: its CORRELATIONAL association with a property (co-occurrence across natural objects) and its CAUSAL effect on the property of GENERATED objects when the feature is clamped during generation. Features where these disagree - strong correlation but weak causal effect, or strong causal effect with weak correlation - are 'discrepant' and, we hypothesize, are enriched for spurious (confounded) or previously-uncatalogued causal design rules. We instantiate this on ESM-2 protein LMs and a SMILES chemistry LM with residual-stream SAEs, using cheap in-silico property evaluators (DSSP/ESMFold, GRAVY, thermostability probes; RDKit logP/QED/functional groups). For each discrepant feature we generate a design-rule hypothesis and independently adjudicate it with a physics-based counterfactual test - constructing matched object pairs that differ only in the feature-linked structural element and measuring the property with an oracle NOT derived from the model - to determine whether the model's causal verdict or the correlational rule is correct. We report the rate and structure of discrepancies, their enrichment for known confounded rules (positive controls), and case studies of candidate novel causal rules. The framework turns feature interventions into an auditable engine for discovering and stress-testing scientific design rules.
Experiments:
SHARED SETUP. Models (frozen): ESM-2 150M/650M with a TopK SAE (k=32, dictionary 16,384) on the residual stream (intrinsic-dimension-elbow layer) and a GPT-style SMILES chemistry LM (~10M) with a residual-stream SAE; a Matryoshka SAE variant for robustness. SAEs trained on 20M activation-tokens from 500k-object subsets, 3 SAE seeds. Feature bank: interpretable, property-linked features selected by concept-correlation/probe AUROC on held-out natural objects. Cheap evaluators on FINISHED objects: proteins - alpha-helix/beta-sheet % (DSSP on ESMFold), GRAVY, molecular weight, a thermostability proxy (light fine-tuned head), motif presence (HMMER/regex); molecules - RDKit logP, QED, ring/aromatic counts, specific functional groups (SMARTS). For each (feature, property) pair: a Correlational score (point-biserial / mutual information between feature activation and property over a large natural sample) and a Causal score (property change per unit steer at low strength within the validity budget, from a strength sweep with unsteered and norm-matched random-direction controls; validity gated by pseudo-perplexity/pLDDT or RDKit-validity). Generation seeds: 5.

Experiment 1 (H1 - discrepant features are numerous): Tests whether plotting correlational vs causal score surfaces many features where the two disagree. Decisive metric: discrepancy rate = fraction of (feature, property) pairs whose residual from the correlation=causation diagonal exceeds a noise band set by test-retest variance of the two scores. Convincing result: discrepancy rate >= 15% of pairs, with the off-diagonal mass beyond the noise band. Decision band: discrepancy rate in [5%, 15%] -> discrepancies exist but are uncommon. Negative result (< 5%, i.e. correlation tracks causation) is itself valuable, establishing that interpretable features faithfully track causal design rules, and refutes H1. Quadrants reported: (A) high-corr/low-causal (candidate spurious), (B) low-corr/high-causal (candidate uncatalogued causal), (C) concordant; rates broken out per domain, model size, SAE variant.

Experiment 2 (H2 - discrepancies are enriched for genuinely non-causal rules): Tests whether the discrepancy map recovers KNOWN spurious rules and whether an independent physics oracle sides with the model over the textbook on adjudicated cases. Decisive metric: agreement rate between the model's causal verdict and an independent physics adjudication on a sample of discrepant pairs. Convincing result: the discrepancy filter attains precision >= 0.7 on a labeled set (known-spurious rules landing in quadrant A, known-causal in C), AND physics adjudication agrees with the model's causal verdict on >= 70% of adjudicated discrepancies. Decision band: precision or agreement in [0.5, 0.7] -> partial validation. Negative result (near-chance precision/agreement) refutes H2. Data: a literature-curated set of known confounded and known causal structure-property associations (as many as the literature supports across both domains); matched counterfactual object pairs differing only in the feature-linked structural element (single-motif insert/delete or point substitutions for proteins; minimal SMARTS edits with matched scaffolds for molecules); the adjudication oracle (FoldX/Rosetta or MD-lite for proteins; RDKit/empirical logP or docking for molecules) is deliberately independent of the generative model's training signal; matching quality reported.

Experiment 3 (H3 - discrepancies are a design-rule engine): Tests whether quadrant-B causal-but-low-correlation features act as design levers where correlational-only rules fail. Decisive metric: success rate of producing the target property in NEW designs when steering the causal (quadrant-B) feature versus applying the correlational-only rule. Convincing result: causal-rule success >= 2x correlational-only success and >= 0.10 absolute. Decision band: causal-rule success between 1.2x and 2x correlational-only -> a real but modest advantage. Negative result (causal rules no better than correlational) refutes H3. Auto-generated human-readable candidate rules (feature label + measured causal effect) are the deliverable; robustness reported across two model sizes, two SAE architectures, and both domains.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) In-silico correlational and causal scores and physics adjudicators are all imperfect proxies; the strongest claim is triangulated agreement/disagreement among independent in-silico signals, not wet-lab truth. To reduce circularity, the adjudication oracle is deliberately chosen to be independent of the generative model's training signal. 2) Discrepancies could arise from SAE artifacts (entangled features, poor reconstruction) rather than genuine causal/correlational structure; we mitigate with multiple SAE architectures, probe verification, and random-direction controls. 3) Constructing clean matched counterfactuals is hard, especially for proteins where a single edit can change many things; we restrict to minimal, well-controlled edits and report matching quality. 4) The positive-control set of known spurious/causal rules may be small, limiting enrichment power; we include as many labeled rules as the literature supports across both domains. 5) A feature's causal score depends on layer/strength; we sweep strength within the validity budget and test layer sensitivity. 6) If discrepancies turn out to be rare (correlation almost always matches causation), that is itself a valuable, publishable result establishing that interpretable features faithfully track causal design rules.
